newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-NORTH-EAST STREWS CASH ON GLORY TRAIL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-NORTH-EAST STREWS CASH ON GLORY TRAIL.

text.p: There are 80 million good reasons why the fans of north-east rivals Newcastle United and Middlesbrough would like to see their teams posing with silverware at the end of the season.

For that is the number of pounds sterling that the neighbouring clubs' respective managers, old England team mates Kevin Keegan and Bryan Robson, have spent on assembling two of the most exciting squads in English soccer.

As a result of that huge outlay -- which does not include the millions spent modernising St James' Park or building Middlesbrough's new Riverside Stadium -- Sunday's Tyne-Tees derby should be even more impassioned than usual. This time, far more than just local pride is at stake.
With the region's other neighbour Sunderland also recently promoted and having their new stadium built in time for next season, these are exciting times for the north-east of England.
For the first time since the 1976-77 season all three clubs are in the top division and, while Newcastle are in the vanguard of change, Middlesbrough and Sunderland are also building for success.
Keegan has spent around 55 million pounds ($88 million) on new players.

They include Alan Shearer, who cost a world record fee of 15 million pounds ($24 million) when he signed for his home-town club from Blackburn in July, Colombian Faustino Asprilla, who came from Parma last January for a fee of 7.5 million ($12 million), and striker Les Ferdinand, who arrived from Queen's Park Rangers in exchange for six million ($9.5 million) at the start of last season.

Robson, who has paid out approximately 25 million pounds ($40 million), made his most expensive signing when Fabrizio Ravanelli completed something of a surreal move from Juventus in July for seven million ($11.25 million) while Brazilians Juninho and Emerson cost 8.75 million ($14 million) between them.
None of those moves would have been possible without the largesse of two men -- Newcastle chairman Sir John Hall and Middlesbrough's young millionaire owner Steve Gibson.

They have helped transform Newcastle and Middlesbrough from clubs which were locked into the past and going nowhere fast into honour-chasing outfits. Indeed Middlesbrough went into liquidation 10 years ago and were only saved from extinction at the last minute.

Now Hall and Gibson, along with some of the most passionate soccer fans anywhere in the world, would like to see a return on their money with their clubs winning the trophies which have proved to be so elusive.

The north-east has always been regarded as English soccer's hotbed, producing more talented youngsters and more impassioned supporters than any other region in the country -- including Liverpool or Manchester.
The paradox is that Newcastle, Middlesbrough and Sunderland have always bought in players from outside the region while the best players from the north-east have played for other teams.
The most famous examples are Bobby and Jack Charlton, both born 18 miles from Newcastle but whose careers were spent at Manchester United and Leeds respectively.

But there was also 'Boro manager Robson, who was born halfway between Newcastle and Sunderland yet played the bulk of his career with Manchester United, not to mention Shearer himself, who went for a trial at Newcastle as a schoolboy, was not selected and began his career 200 miles away at Southampton.
All of them won cups or championships -- but no north-east club has had its name engraved on a major trophy since Sunderland won the F.A. Cup in 1973.

Newcastle's last major success came when they won the old Inter Cities Fairs Cup in 1969. They captured their last major domestic trophy in 1955 when they lifted the F.A. Cup for the third time in five seasons. Middlesbrough have never won the league, Cup or the league cup.

Newcastle looked like ending their long barren spell last season when they led the title race by 12 points in January -- but a slump in form towards the end of the season allowed Manchester United to pip them for the crown instead.

This season they look a more mature, tougher outfit, and although Shearer will be missing on Sunday following a groin operation, the likes of David Ginola, Ferdinand and Asprilla should find a way through Middlesbrough's defence -- the leakiest in the league.
Middlesbrough started last season well but also faded and, so far this season, have done little to suggest their 120-year search for the league title title will end.

However, with Ravanelli currently leading the scoring charts with 13 goals in all competitions and Emerson and Juninho creating plenty of chances, Middlesbrough look a better bet for one of the cups than the title.
